title: The role of weather conditions on running performance in the Boston Marathon from 1972 to 2018
authors: Knechtle B, Di Gangi S, Rust CA, Villiger E, Rosemann T, Nikolaidis PT
population: Boston Marathon 1972-2018: 580,990 observations from 382,209 finishers (all runners, near-elite 101-200 and 21-100, annual top ten, annual winners), generalized additive mixed models
findings: Each 1 C rise in average air temperature was associated with worse performance by 1:47 (h:min:sec) for all finishers and 0:20 for annual winners.
WBGT and pressure, when increasing, were also related to worse performance.
Tail wind improved performance in all groups; increasing wind speed and precipitation worsened performance in most groups (precipitation excepted for winners).
Men were faster than women in all groups, with the sex difference largest in near-elite groups.
limitations: Single race (course effects); multivariable model with collinear weather terms; average finishing time not in the abstract, so the percent-per-C scale is only illustrative; air temperature rather than WBGT drives the headline slope; pressure effect conflicts with El Helou 2012.
implications: Corroborates a roughly 5-fold larger per-degree time loss for the whole field than for winners (107 s vs 20 s per C; for a hypothetical 4 h finisher about 0.7%/C, for a 2:10 winner about 0.26%/C, own arithmetic), supporting an ability multiplier above 1 for non-elite runners.
Add wind (headwind and speed) as an optional adjustment term; no numeric values are justified beyond the direction.
Do not use the per-C air-temperature slope as a WBGT slope; keep the two separate.
